US and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on Iran
Multinational ‘anti-war bloc’ uses Istanbul summit to call for a diplomatic solution to Middle East crisis
Foreign ministers at a summit of eight European and Middle Eastern countries have urged the US and Israel not to renews their attacks on Iran, warning a fresh outbreak of fighting would spread conflict and push oil prices even higher.
The development of a new multinational “anti-war bloc” represents a challenge to the increasingly open plans by the US and Israel to relaunch strikes on Iran while talks on Tehran’s nuclear programme remain deadlocked.
The Turkish foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, joint convener of the summit in Istanbul, said: “Military intervention in Iran is not any kind of solution. We agreed that a new military attack would spread the war and the conflict in the region. All the countries around the table do not want the war to spread even more, once again.”
Ministers also demanded an end to the Houthi assaults on Saudi Arabia, and an immediate opening of the strait of Hormuz currently blockaded by Iranian ships and drones.
Jean-Noël Barrot, the French foreign minister, said another war between Iran and the US would be bad for both sides, and only worsen rising oil prices, which have hit their highest level since May. Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, also urged both sides to embrace diplomacy.
The Istanbul meeting, an unprecedented gathering of regional and European leaders initiated by Turkey and Germany , represented a rare chance for European ministers to have any input into the crises afflicting the Middle East, including in Yemen, Palestine and Iran. They have largely been left as bystanders, apart from sending air force protection to Saudi Arabia as it tries to fend off Houthi drone and missile assaults on its airports and energy installations.
The Middle Eastern states were represented by Fidan, Egypt’s Badr Abdelatty, Pakistan’s Ishaq Dar and Saudi Arabia’s Faisal bin Farhan. Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia formed the Mecca defensive security pact in August, a grouping Egypt may join.
The European side was represented by Barrot, Miliband, Germany’s Johann Wadephul and Italy’s Antonio Tajani. The agenda covered the Palestinian issue, including settlement expansion, settler violence and the two-state solution, as well as security in the strait of Hormuz, Yemen and efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war and prevent spillover into the Black Sea.
Wadephul said: “We are united by the impact these deadlocked conflicts are having on the economy and security of our countries and by the will to seek new ways to bring about solutions.”
He made no criticism of the US but accused “the Houthis and Iran of blackmailing world trade and continuing to stranglehold global supplies of energy and fertiliser”.
“We are feeling the effects of the attacks on shipping routes and whether at the petrol pump or the supermarket,” he said. “Elsewhere there is threat of famine.”
Tajani said the aim of the meeting was to work for “de-escalation to guarantee freedom of navigation”.
“I do not believe the problem can be solved from a purely military standpoint,” he added. “If we want to reopen Hormuz, which is vital for our economies, we must promote dialogue and make Iran understand that this attitude cannot continue.”

items.title: If a Stock Market Crash Is on the Way, Warren Buffett Says This Is the Best Thing Investors Can Do for Their Portfolio - The Motley Fool
items.summary: If a Stock Market Crash Is on the Way, Warren Buffett Says This Is the Best Thing Investors Can Do for Their Portfolio  The Motley Fool
items.content:
The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -0.52% ) and Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC -0.21% ) have recently been experiencing a bout of volatility after repeatedly notching record highs throughout 2026. With stocks coming under pressure, some investors are wondering whether a larger market correction is approaching.
Part of the concern stems from elevated bond yields and stubborn inflation. Meanwhile, artificial intelligence (AI) hyperscalers like Amazon , Microsoft , Alphabet , and Meta Platforms are among the companies supporting the broader economy as they accelerate spending on data centers .
Whether this volatility is just a temporary pullback or the beginning of something worse is impossible to know. But legendary investor Warren Buffett spent decades explaining how to navigate markets dominated by exciting new technologies, sky-high valuations, and uncertainty.
Former Berkshire Hathaway CEO Warren Buffett. Image source: Getty Images.
Revolutionary technology does not equal a good investment
Buffett built Berkshire Hathaway  into one of history's most successful investment firms simply because he had a relentless focus on businesses he understands. He generally avoided technology stocks, instead favoring industries such as insurance, banking, consumer products, utilities, and energy. These businesses usually have relatively predictable economics, which allowed Buffett to better assess their long-term earnings potential.
Buffett understood that an industry can revolutionize society without producing attractive returns overall. Consider the automobile and aviation industries as examples. Cars and airplanes have unquestionably transformed the global economy, but countless early manufacturers and airlines have gone bankrupt as competition intensified.
The theme here is that identifying which industries are game changers is much easier than choosing the specific companies that will capture profits in the long run. This distinction matters in today's AI environment.
While AI is shaping up to be one of the most transformative technologies in history, that doesn't mean every semiconductor company, software developer, or infrastructure provider is going to generate market-beating returns.
Is the AI revolution destined to end up like the dot-com bubble?
During the late 1990s, investors were pouring money into virtually anything that resembled the internet. Speculative technology stocks became multibaggers , even when the underlying companies had little revenue, no profits, or incomplete business models.
Reality inevitably caught up with expectations. After peaking in March 2000, the Nasdaq plummeted by 78% by October 2002. Suddenly, once-promising internet businesses left investors holding the bag.
Today, some investors are worried the AI boom could become a modern retelling of the dot-com bubble. Sure, AI leaders like Nvidia and the cloud hyperscalers already generate substantial profits and cash flow. The reason why is that their AI infrastructure is supported by numerous established businesses rather than simply promises around future growth. Still, the industry faces uncertainty because not every model developer is going to succeed in the long run.
This brings us to Buffett's most important investing principle. The single best thing an investor can do for their portfolio right now is load up on companies with durable competitive advantages rather than chasing the stocks attracting the most attention. Buffett describes these advantages as economic moats that come in the form of powerful brands, high switching costs, network effects , and economies of scale.
There's a more subtle lesson investors can learn from the dot-com crash: Time in the market is more valuable than trying to time the market. Suppose you invested in the S&P 500 near its peak during the dot-com era. If you managed to stay invested, you would have witnessed the index appreciate roughly 450%.
A hypothetical $10,000 investment would have grown to nearly $55,000, even though it was made right before a major market collapse. What's even more inspiring is that over the last 25 years, the S&P 500 has endured three recessions -- pictured above as the grey-shaded columns -- and managed to come out higher after each one. This underscores the resiliency of the S&P 500 as one of the greatest wealth-creation vehicles.
This performance is why Buffett's emphasis on diversification is both valuable and relevant in today's market. Rather than panic-selling whenever stocks become volatile or valuation is frothy, investors should rebalance their portfolios if their positions expose them to unnecessary risk.
Ultimately, no one knows whether the recent sell-off will permeate into a full-blown crash. But Buffett's philosophy offers a practical response: The best opportunity is to own quality businesses, avoid paying unreasonable prices, and remain patient enough to let compounding do the heavy lifting.

Tankers part of US-Russia deal that could see 500,000 metric tonnes of fuel supplied to world market this month. What we know on day 1,704
Three tankers carrying Russian diesel are on their ⁠way to North America, Russian deputy prime minister Alexander Novak said ⁠on Friday . In ​a statement quoted by Russian news agencies, Novak said the cargoes were ⁠part of a deal that could see Russian companies supply 500,000 metric tonnes to US and world markets in October. “The first ⁠three fuel tankers are already on their ​way to the eastern ‌coast of ‌the Atlantic Ocean, with significant support from the ‌RDIF (Russian Direct Investment Fund),” Novak said. Under a deal announced this month by US president Donald Trump, Russia agreed ‌to supply diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel ​prices in return for Trump temporarily lifting US sanctions on Russian fuel. Reuters reported that the Malta-flagged ⁠medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes, loaded with ultra-low sulphur diesel, is expected to arrive in ‌the US on 7 November.
The White House has said that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky , where a deepening humanitarian crisis has left thousands of civilians struggling to survive. In a statement on Friday, the White House said both sides had agreed to halt all military operations in the city from 27 October to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and preparations for the evacuation of civilians. Residents of the southern Ukrainian city, which has been under Russian occupation since February 2022, have described increasingly desperate conditions amid severe shortages of food, water and electricity. An estimated 2,000 people remain in the city, with some reportedly forced to survive on weeds, boiled grass, bread and meagre rations. Both Russian and Ukrainian officials said all sides were close to agreeing to a ceasefire.
The Oleshky ceasefire comes as the US is trying to organise new talks aimed at ending the war . Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Friday negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the US have agreed to technical-level meetings in the first half of November in Abu Dhabi. A US official later said the three ⁠countries may hold their next talks in a couple weeks in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland. Zelenskyy said he hoped a meeting of the countries’ leaders would follow.
The peace efforts follow a rift between Washington and Kyiv in recent weeks and a series of moves by Trump seen as favouring Russia, including limitations being placed on the Starlink communication system that Ukraine uses to protect against incoming attacks. Trump said on Friday that if Ukraine still faced a problem accessing the system, he would straighten it out ​and, if necessary, speak about the matter to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
As the UK government prepares next week for the first budget under Andy Burnham’s leadership, EU leaders have pressed the new prime minister at a summit in Brussels to contribute more to Ukraine’s defence effort . EU officials say Canada and Japan also should do more to support Ukraine .
The UN nuclear watchdog IAEA said ⁠Fiday ​that repairs to key ⁠power infrastructure near Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia ⁠nuclear power ​plant ‌had been completed ‌ under a ‌temporary ceasefire it brokered. The repairs strengthened the plant’s connection ‌to its sole remaining external power ​line, known as Ferosplavna-1, reducing the ⁠risk of another ​loss of ​off-site ​electricity at ​Europe’s largest ‌nuclear ​power ​station.

Oil price rises above $117 a barrel amid fears US will renew strikes on Iran
Brent crude increase follows Tehran threatening retaliatory attacks on Gulf refineries and datacentres
Oil has hit its highest level in more than six months as fears of fresh escalation in the Middle East conflict grip the energy markets.
Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, rose by about 3.5% on Friday to pass $117 a barrel at one point – its highest level since April.
The jump came after Tehran said it would attack oil facilities, undersea cables, datacentres and AI facilities in the Gulf region if a new US-Israeli offensive was launched against Iran .
Richard Hunter, of the broker Interactive Investor, said: “Widespread reports that the US is considering renewed military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections rather than pursuing a diplomatic route was enough for the price to pop, after what many had considered would be a brief conflict is now in its eighth month.”
The oil price later eased back slight to sit about 2.7% up at just over $116 a barrel. Brent crude had traded at about $72 a barrel back in February, before the Iran war began, but soared to touch $126 a barrel by the end of April.
Tensions in the region have been rising this week and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps claimed to have struck four commercial ships in the strait of Hormuz on Wednesday. The US state department ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia , which has faced continued attacks from Houthi rebels in Yemen.
Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at the broker Wealth Club, said fears were rising that American and Israeli forces would be ordered to launch strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure after the US elections on 3 November.
She added: “At the same time, the attacks on Saudi Arabia’s facilities by Houthi rebels have intensified this week, and for ships attempting to cross the strait of Hormuz, it’s still a dangerous journey, with projectiles still being fired.”
Streeter said Ukraine’s bombardment of Russian diesel refineries was also adding to supply concerns.

Saudi Arabia wants to send 10 million barrels of oil a day around Hormuz. A former Treasury official says it may barely move prices
Saudi oil giant Aramco , officially the Saudi Arabian Oil Company, is racing to build a bigger back door around the Strait of Hormuz.
Aramco CEO Amin Nasser said this week that the company is working to raise the capacity of its East-West Crude Oil Pipeline, also known as the Petroline, to 10 million barrels a day from about 7 million today, while running engineering studies on additional export routes. Nasser made the comments to Al Arabiya Business in his first interview since the war began . The plan echoes an announcement earlier this month from Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, who told the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh that the expansion would take two to three years .
The goal is to reduce the kingdom’s reliance on the Strait of Hormuz, which has been largely choked off since the U.S. and Israel launched a joint military attack on Iran on Feb. 28. Saudi crude production fell below 7 million barrels a day for much of the war’s first six months, down from more than 10 million before the conflict, and recovered to about 8 million in September, according to the International Energy Agency .
The Petroline spans Saudi Arabia, running roughly 750 miles from the Abqaiq processing hub near the Persian Gulf to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea . Before the war, it typically carried around 2 million barrels a day. Aramco ramped it up within weeks, and the line hit its full 7 million-barrel capacity by late March, with about 2 million of those barrels feeding Saudi refineries rather than export markets. The pipeline helped Aramco post a 25% jump in first-quarter profit . Adding another 3 million barrels a day would be a major undertaking.
But it may have little tangible impact on world fuel prices, according to Gilbert Metcalf , a visiting professor at the MIT Sloan School of Management and a former deputy assistant secretary for environment and energy at the U.S. Treasury Department.
“If—and this is a big if—the Saudis can increase pipeline flow to 10 million barrels per day, it will put about 2% more oil into the global marketplace,” Metcalf tells Fortune . “That could lower prices a bit, but there’s a lot of uncertainty here. The pipeline is vulnerable to drone and missile attacks, as is much of the Saudi petroleum infrastructure. And it’s not entirely clear that there is available refinery capacity to process the oil.”
That vulnerability isn’t hypothetical. The Petroline was first hit in May 2019, when Houthi drones struck a pumping station . This year it has been attacked repeatedly. An April 9 strike on a pumping station cut throughput by about 700,000 barrels a day before Saudi Arabia restored full capacity days later. On Sept. 10, drones struck the line in the Riyadh and Medina regions; Saudi officials said they were launched from Iraq . The attack forced a precautionary shutdown that lasted until Sept. 22, according to Kpler . And a Saudi energy-sector source told AFP that an Oct. 4 attack on a pumping station in Khurais halted flows again , though Bloomberg reported that oil continued to move.
The Red Sea end of the route is under pressure, too. Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia in July, have repeatedly attacked Saudi tankers, and in September seized control of the area around the Bab al-Mandab Strait , the southern gateway to the Red Sea. Southbound tankers leaving Yanbu must pass through it.
Even if the pipeline runs smoothly, a bigger Petroline might do little to ease the world’s dependence on Hormuz. “I don’t think moving more oil to the pipeline takes much pressure off opening the Strait of Hormuz,” Metcalf says. “Despite what the U.S. Treasury and Energy Departments are saying, it does not appear that oil is flowing through Hormuz at anywhere near levels observed before the U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran. Add to that threats in the Bab al-Mandab Strait and it’s clear that risks for Saudi oil production are as high now as they’ve ever been.”
Tanker data supports his skepticism. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said this month that Gulf crude flows had recovered to between 80% and 90% of prewar levels. But Kpler figures show oil exports through Hormuz averaged just under 9 million barrels a day in September , roughly 44% of February’s level. Gulf producers are pursuing longer-term workarounds as well: the UAE is fast-tracking a new pipeline of its own .
The Saudi government owns about 81.5% of Aramco. The kingdom’s sovereign wealth fund, the Public Investment Fund, holds 16%, and roughly 2.5% trades publicly . It is the world’s largest oil company and a major natural gas producer, with plans to raise gas output 80% by 2030 from 2021 levels. Yet even Aramco’s scale and an expanded pipeline may not be enough to shift the balance of power in the Middle East.
“The irony is that the balance of regional power has tilted from Saudi Arabia towards Iran as a result of the attacks on Iran,” Metcalf says. “This would have been unthinkable just a year ago.”

Despite hopes for a pause in escalation after President Trump signaled no further attacks on Iran before the midterms, conflict across the Middle East persisted. Coupled with a larger-than-expected inventory draw, the unrest helped drive December futures higher.
While US President Trump pledged not to continue attacking Iran until after the midterms, the conflicts in the Middle East raged on leading December futures prices to continue November's rally. An unexpectedly high inventory draw only added upward momentum. WTI's High was Tuesday's $110.50/bbl which was November's settlement day and the result of traders closing out positions. The Low was Wednesday's $96.25, the first day of trading for December. Brent crude hit its High on Friday at $116.35/bbl with the low on Tuesday at $105.95. Both grades settled higher on the week. The WTI/Brent spread has blown out to $14.00.
Iran continues to attack vessels in the Strait of Hormuz despite the halt of US attacks on them. Both crude tankers and regular cargo ships have been hit recently. They have further threatened increased aggression in the area should the US and Israel resume their strikes on Iran. The US has stepped-up its presence in the region with a third aircraft carrier and more Marines.
Meanwhile, the Yemeni-Houthi/Saudi Arabia conflict has escalated. Houthis have hit large metropolitan areas within Saudi Arabia including, the headquarters of Saudi Aramco, as well as one oilfield. Saudi troops have made their way into Yemen and the Saudi Air Force has attacked the country's capital.
Despite the military actions on both sides, oil does continue to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with Kpler estimating as much as a 24 million b/d last week. Globally, however, a deficit in actual refined products remains the bigger issue. Less refined product leaving the Persian Gulf and the continuing Ukrainian attacks on Russian refiners are largely responsible for the shortfall.
Tanker-tracker service, Kpler, confirmed the loading of a Russian tanker with ultra-low sulfur diesel bound for NYC with an expected arrival date of Nove. 7, the first delivery under Pres. Trump's recent deal with Putin. And tanker rates have risen to about $20/bbl all-in which is 7 times higher than a year-ago. Factors such as risk premium, day rates, the increase in ship-to-ship transfers and maritime insurance rates have all played a hand in the increases.
Given the increased demand for diesel, US refineries have been running at the highest operating rates since 1998. From May through September, utilization averaged 65%. However, total available capacity is down 4% since 2019. Two refineries in California were shut down in just the past year. US refiners have been recording record high crack margins over the past 5 months. And, despite being past the peak summer demand period and the need for periodic maintenance, refinery utilization remains above 90%.
The US Energy Information Administration's (EIA) Weekly Petroleum Status Report indicated that commercial crude oil inventories last week decreased while the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) held at 283 million bbl (the lowest level since 1982). Production last week fell again by 300,000 b/d to 13.3 million b/d vs. 13.7 million b/d the prior week and 13.6 million b/d last year.
The higher energy prices are weighing on financial markets as stocks fall and treasury yields drop. Jobless claims last week dropped 6,000 to 194,000 vs. an expected 200,000. Housing starts last month were down 5.2% from August while pending home sales were down 7.3%. The Manufacturing PMI was 56 as activity continues to expand. Consumer sentiment remains weak at 48%. The Dow dipped on Friday but was positive on the week while the NASDAQ and S&P were lower. Gold settled down while the USD made slight gains.
December WTI NYMEX futures carried forward November's momentum have shot past the Upper-Bollinger Band limit and well-above their 8-, 13, and 20-day Moving Averages on the rally which broke the $103 mark. Volume is about the recent average at 292,000. The Relative Strength Indicator (RSI), a momentum indicator, is very oversold at 75. Resistance is now pegged at $103.50 while near-term Support is $102.50 (Bollinger Band).
In the short-term, nothing appears to point to any easing of hostilities in the Middle East. Iran has no incentive to cease attacking ships and the Yemeni-Houthis have successfully attacked key Saudi Arabian sites. It may take an earlier intervention than planned by the US. The refined product shortages will be with us for a while yet and, at some point US refiners will have to reduce their utilization for routine maintenance as well as the turnaround to winter blending.
The next 2 weeks look very bearish for heating oil demand along in the Northeast.
November NYMEX natural gas futures prices this week tanked as production continues to increase but the normal seasonal temperatures have yet to materialize across the country. Additionally, there was an above-average storage injection. The week's High was $3.18/MMbtu on Monday and while the Low was Friday's $2.62. Natural gas demand this week has been estimated at 104.5 bcfd with lower power consumption while supply was thought to be 117 bcfd. LNG exports hit a new high of 19.8 bcfd while exports to Mexico were 6.8 bcfd.
European natural gas prices rose to levels not seen since 2022 over concerns regarding LNG supplies heading into winter. In the UK, natural gas prices at the NBP were most recently higher at $30.65/MMbtu. Dutch TTF futures were also higher at $29.60/MMbtu. Asia's JKM was quoted at $30.63/MMbtu as Asian and European markets are essentially competing for the same shipments. The highest prices in 4 years. EU gas storage levels currently stand at only 75%. The EIA's Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report indicated an injection of 77 bcf vs. a forecast of +80 bcf and a 5-year average of +70 bcf. Total gas in storage is now 3.644 tcf, 4.0% below last year and 1.0% above the 5-year average.
November 2026 NYMEX Henry Hub Natural Gas futures have fallen below the Lower-Bollinger Band and the 8-, 13- & 20-day Moving Averages. Volume is below the recent average at 125. The RSI is very oversold at 30. Support is $2.60 with Resistance at $2.73 (Bollinger Band).
Natural gas production remains fairly steady while above-normal temperatures have delayed the start of the normal fall demand. LNG exports should stay strong given global demand and pricing. The storage surplus vs. the 5-year average continues to shrink. At 3.644 tcf with only 2 weeks remaining in the official storage injection season, it would take 178 bcf/week to hit the 4.0 tcf mark by Nov. 1.

items.title: Trump Invokes Cold War-Era Law to Boost Oil Refining as Gas Prices Soar - Law Commentary
items.summary: Trump Invokes Cold War-Era Law to Boost Oil Refining as Gas Prices Soar  Law Commentary
items.content:
Trump Invokes Cold War-Era Law to Boost Oil Refining as Gas Prices Soar
President Donald Trump has invoked a Cold War-era defense law to direct up to $150 million toward U.S. oil refineries as gasoline prices climb above $4 a gallon and diesel exceeds $6. The October 22 action allows the federal government to support refinery expansion and petroleum infrastructure projects under powers intended to protect national defense.
The administration's plan draws on a broader $1 billion congressional allocation for energy projects considered critical to national security. The Department of Energy expects the investments to add millions of gallons of gasoline, diesel and jet fuel to daily domestic production, although funding recipients and project timelines have yet to be announced.
Trump signed a presidential memorandum directing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to use Section 303 of the Defense Production Act of 1950 to strengthen domestic petroleum production, refining, pipelines and fuel storage facilities. The order identifies those operations as essential to national defense and authorizes federal purchases, financial commitments and agreements to expand industrial capacity.
The directive comes as global energy disruptions linked to the conflict involving Iran and attacks on Russian energy infrastructure continue to pressure fuel markets. As of October 23, the national average price of gasoline stood at approximately $4.29 per gallon, while diesel averaged $6.32, increasing transportation and operating costs for consumers and businesses.
Trump determined that financing constraints, construction timelines, permitting delays and supply chain limitations have prevented private industry from expanding petroleum infrastructure quickly enough to meet national defense needs. Trump cited the risk of a petroleum shortfall that could severely impair national defense capabilities.
The president also waived six statutory requirements governing federal support for industrial expansion, citing the national energy emergency he declared in January 2025. Section 303 of the Defense Production Act allows the government to support industries essential to national defense through purchases, financial commitments and investments in production capacity. Enacted during the Korean War, the statute permits specified requirements to be waived during a declared national emergency or when an industrial shortage threatens defense capabilities.
Trump previously invoked the same provision on April 20, designating domestic petroleum production, refining and distribution as essential to national defense. That determination assigned implementation to the energy secretary, while the October 22 memorandum directs Hegseth to carry out the authority.
The Energy Department's latest funding initiative would support efforts to restore and expand American refineries. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the funding would help restart and expand U.S. refining operations.
Federal funding could accelerate expansions at existing refineries, although industry specialists expect substantial increases in fuel production to take months. Equipment purchases, construction and regulatory approvals remain among the obstacles facing operators.
Any relief at the pump could take longer. Gasoline and diesel prices remain tied to global crude oil costs and supply disruptions, limiting how quickly expanded U.S. refining operations could affect what consumers pay.
The Energy Department has yet to identify funding recipients or establish a timeline for the refinery expansions. Project selections will be the next step in determining how quickly the administration's $150 million initiative translates into additional fuel production.

items.title: Federal Reserve Votes Unanimously to Raise Rates 25 Basis Points to 3.75%-4.00%; Warsh Defies White House Pressure to Launch Tightening Cycle - BigGo Finance
items.summary: Federal Reserve Votes Unanimously to Raise Rates 25 Basis Points to 3.75%-4.00%; Warsh Defies White House Pressure to Launch Tightening Cycle  BigGo Finance
items.content:
Federal Reserve Votes Unanimously to Raise Rates 25 Basis Points to 3.75%-4.00%; Warsh Defies White House Pressure to Launch Tightening Cycle
The Federal Open Market Committee voted 12-0 to raise the federal funds rate target range by 25 basis points to 3.75%-4.00%, the first rate hike since July 2023 and the first tightening under Chair Kevin Warsh. August nonfarm payrolls rose by 162,000, far exceeding expectations, while CPI rose 0.4% month-over-month and core CPI rose 0.3%, both above forecasts, providing the basis for the hike. The dot plot shows most members expect one more rate increase this year. White House core officials had publicly opposed a hike, with Trump saying rates should be below 1%. Deutsche Bank expects the Fed to hold steady in October and raise rates by 25 basis points each in December and next March.
Federal Reserve Kevin Warsh Federal Open Market Committee Trump Deutsche Bank Core PCE Consumer Price Index Nonfarm Payrolls Quantitative Easing Artificial Intelligence European Central Bank Bank of Japan
At 2 p.m. EDT on Sept. 16 (Wednesday), the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) voted 12-0 to raise the federal funds rate target range by 25 basis points to 3.75%-4.00%. This is the Federal Reserve's first rate hike since July 2023 and the first under Kevin Warsh as Fed chair, marking the start of a new tightening cycle.
Markets initially reacted relatively calmly after the decision: the S&P 500 and Nasdaq were still higher before Warsh's press conference began, while the Dow was down just 0.1%. But as Warsh stressed at the press conference that inflation is "too high, and has been too high for too long," the three major indexes turned lower and closed in the red — the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell more than 600 points (1.2%), the S&P 500 lost 0.5%, and the Nasdaq closed slightly lower. The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield rose to about 5.01% from 4.95% after the decision, after touching 5.04% intraday the previous day, the highest since 2007. The dollar index rose 0.59% and broke through the 100 mark, while international gold prices came under pressure. For American households, the mortgage burden is more direct: the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate has risen to 7.19%, up about 38 basis points from after Warsh's Jackson Hole speech on Aug. 28 and more than a percentage point higher than a year ago.
Jobs and Inflation Data Together Locked In the Hike
The core driver of the rate increase was a dense batch of economic data released in September. On Sept. 4, U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data showed August nonfarm payrolls rose by 162,000, far exceeding the market expectation of 56,000, with the unemployment rate holding at a historically low 4.1%. The strong labor market gave the Fed room to tighten policy.
Inflation data released afterward further confirmed the need for a hike. The August producer price index (PPI) rose 0.4% month-over-month, with the year-over-year gain accelerating to 5.4% from 4.8% in July, slightly above the expected 5.3%. The August consumer price index (CPI) rose 3.4% year-over-year, in line with both the prior reading and expectations, but the month-over-month gain jumped sharply to 0.4% from 0.1%, the largest monthly increase since May; core CPI rose 0.3% month-over-month, above the expected 0.2% and the biggest gain in four months. Energy CPI surged 16.30% year-over-year, gasoline prices jumped 3.9% month-over-month, and core services inflation excluding housing rose 0.51% month-over-month, the highest level since January.
" inflation remains elevated. Today's policy action will help bring inflation back to the Committee's 2% goal more quickly," Warsh said at the news conference. He added, "It is hard to say that overall financial conditions are restrictive. Most Committee members agree with that, so we have taken back some of the easing."
According to the latest dot plot, the median forecast for the end of 2026 is 4.1%, revised up 30 basis points from 3.8% in June; the median for the end of 2027 was revised up 50 basis points to 4.1% from 3.6%, effectively erasing the previously expected rate cuts next year. The dot plot does not schedule any rate cuts before 2028, showing only one cut in 2028 and at least one more in 2029. At the July meeting, three members had already voted in favor of raising rates; this time the vote was unanimous.
Of the 18 officials who submitted projections, 12 expect one more rate hike this year (corresponding to 4.125% at the end of 2026), four expect two more hikes, and only two believe rates should stay put; Warsh himself did not submit a rate projection. Views on 2027 are close to a three-way split: eight expect more hikes, six expect rates to stay unchanged, and four expect cuts. The Fed also projects overall PCE inflation of 3.7% this year and core PCE of 3.4%, both revised up 0.1 percentage point from June; core PCE will not return to the 2% target until 2029, a year later than previously estimated.

Note: Median projections come from the Summary of Economic Projections (SEP) released by the Federal Reserve on Sept. 16.
Note: Data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics; prior refers to July data.
White House Pressure and a Test of Fed Independence
The rate decision was made against the backdrop of near-unanimous public opposition from the White House's core team. From President Trump and the vice president to the Treasury secretary and the president's senior economic adviser, officials had publicly urged the Fed not to raise rates, with some even advocating cuts. After the decision, Trump said again that U.S. rates should be below 1% and that lower borrowing costs would benefit the U.S. economy; a White House spokesperson said the Fed's decision to raise rates this time "is not convincing."
The scene is quite similar to late 2018. That was also during a hiking cycle, and then-Fed Chair Jerome Powell, who was nominated by Trump himself, was still publicly criticized by Trump, who said the Fed had "gone crazy." The pressure this time is closely tied to political activity ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections — the cost of living is one of voters' top concerns — but the Fed's decision did not change because of political pressure.
Matthew Luzzetti, chief U.S. economist at Deutsche Bank, noted that the September meeting has laid the groundwork for a path of "skipping October and hiking again in December." The bank expects the Fed to keep rates unchanged at its Oct. 27-28 meeting, then raise rates by 25 basis points each on Dec. 8-9 and next March, for a cumulative additional 50 basis points of tightening.
However, the decision to pause is not itself difficult; the hard part is convincing the market that the Fed will still "see it through." Luzzetti said September inflation data broadly beat expectations and core PCE is expected to rise to 3.1%-3.2% year-over-year, leaving the case for a pause far from sufficient. Warsh, who was already questioned at the July news conference after his remarks were read by the market as a softening of stance, now faces a higher bar for credibility.
Deutsche Bank believes the market's focus will fall on the news conference rather than the statement itself. Warsh needs to work on several fronts at once: explain the logic of a pause, reaffirm the commitment to price stability, clarify the relationship between tighter financial conditions and the policy rate, and offer a characterization of artificial intelligence (AI)-related market volatility.
The rate hike is not an isolated event. The European Central Bank (ECB) raised all three key rates by 25 basis points on Sept. 10, lifting the deposit rate to 2.50%; the Bank of Japan (BOJ) voted 7-2 on Sept. 18 to raise its policy rate by 25 basis points to 1.25%, the highest since 1995. The three major central banks raised rates within eight days of one another, against a common backdrop of energy prices pushed up by fighting in the Middle East and domestic inflation still above target in each economy.
For Asian markets, the policy rate gap between Japan and the U.S. remains more than 2.5 percentage points. The BOJ said after the meeting that it will continue raising rates depending on inflation and yen moves; fluctuations in the yen exchange rate and Japanese government bond yields will be key things to watch.
The market resistance to Fed rate hikes is closely tied to the policy legacy of the 2008 financial crisis. To respond to the subprime crisis, the Fed cut rates to near zero and launched quantitative easing (QE), buying long-term bonds on a large scale to push down long-term rates. Then-Chair Ben Bernanke decided to buy $1.75 trillion of bonds over more than a year, about a quarter of the bonds in circulation at the time.
Around the launch of QE, the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield fell from about 3.7% in September 2008 to about 2.2% in December of that year. A flood of money poured into stocks, and rising asset prices drove real-economy recovery through the wealth effect, while the unemployment rate stopped rising and steadily declined. But this also planted the seeds of the market's "drug dependence." In May 2013, Bernanke merely said he was considering reducing bond purchases, and the bond market panicked and sold off, with the 10-year yield rising more than 100 basis points in half a year — a episode known as the "taper tantrum."
Now, as the Fed shifts from standing pat to raising rates, the market reaction is similarly sharp. Warsh said clearly at the news conference: "I will not give fixed forward guidance, and I will not pre-commit to a future rate path. Every meeting remains data-dependent."
On artificial intelligence, Warsh is expected to reiterate that AI is the most transformative technological advance seen to date. He may note that AI could at some point help suppress inflation through supply-side channels, but in the near term it is supporting demand and adding to inflation pressure. Deutsche Bank believes Warsh will mention the Fed's attention to AI-related valuations and financial stability risks, but the wording will be neutral; the key message is that tighter financial conditions cannot substitute for higher policy rates.
In addition, Warsh previously announced at an International Monetary Fund (IMF) event that the first field hearing of the "Productivity and Employment" working group will be held in the Bay Area on Nov. 16.
For investors, the significance of this hike goes beyond a 25-basis-point change in rates. It is a test of the Fed's credibility under the triple pull of political pressure, market dependence and stubborn inflation. The next FOMC meeting on Dec. 8-9 and the direction of inflation and jobs data will continue to shape global asset pricing.

items.title: Turmoil hits AI buildout as neoclouds face pressure, credit risks mount and Solidigm pulls IPO
items.summary: Stock slumps, pulled IPOs and rising spreads on credit default swaps this week sets stage for hyperscaler earnings.
items.content:
AI turmoil: neoclouds struggle, credit risks jump, Solidigm pulls IPO
Concerns over the AI trade dragged the Nasdaq down this week, with neoclouds posting some of the steepest losses.
Debt markets are roiling, with Meta, Oracle and Nvidia facing the largest-ever spreads on credit default swaps linked to their corporate bonds.
SK Hynix abandoned plans for an IPO of its Solidigm unit.
CoreWeave founder and CEO Mike Intrator poses for a photo during the company's initial public offering at the Nasdaq headquarters in New York, March 28, 2025.
Neoclouds tanked. Credit default swaps soared. Meta turned cash flow negative. And SK Hynix's Solidigm unit canceled plans for its initial public offering.
It's been a rocky week for the AI infrastructure trade.
The Nasdaq followed Thursday's beating with an additional drop on Friday to end the week down 0.7%. Among the hyperscalers, the worst performer was Alphabet , shares of which sank 6% ahead of the internet giant's third-quarter earnings report next week. Microsoft and Amazon are also on the docket, and they each saw shares fall less than 1%.
While the tech market has thus far avoided a dramatic across-the-board sell-off, the artificial intelligence build-out is showing signs of strain.
Shares of neoclouds CoreWeave , Nebius and IREN all fell sharply this week, bringing their losses for October to well over 30% each. CoreWeave, the leader of the pack, has seen spreads on its CDS widen past 11%, generally viewed as a distress level, as investors have to pay up for protection against default.
Meanwhile, yields on the company's 2031 and 2032 unsecured notes topped 15% .
"What investors are doing is throwing every baby out with the bathwater and saying anyone who is a neocloud" will be devalued, Roundhill Investments CEO Dave Mazza told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Thursday.
Roundhill Investments CEO Dave Mazza on the problem with neoclouds
Fears aren't limited to the U.S. market. Shares of Elice Group, a South Korean cloud provider, dropped 30% in their market debut on Tuesday, and shares of Australia's NextDC plunged 39.5% on Wednesday after the data center operator slashed its annual earnings forecast.
AI optimism has been the major market driver for the past couple of years, as unrelenting demand for new models and services pushes the world's biggest tech companies to spend on infrastructure at historic rates. However, skeptics are getting more vocal in their concerns that returns on AI investment won't justify the capital expenditures.
Analysts at research and advisory firm Gartner predict that 80% of neocloud companies will either cease operations or be absorbed by 2030.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , perhaps the leading AI evangelist remains bullish. Huang said this week at a company conference in Berlin that "demand for the neoclouds is off the charts."
"The demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital," Huang told CNBC's Arjun Kharpal . "That's going to get solved."
Wall Street isn't convinced. On Thursday, South Korean memory giant SK Hynix , one of the biggest winners in the AI boom, said it's pulling an IPO for its U.S.-based Solidigm unit, citing market volatility. SK Hynix purchased Solidigm, which makes NAND and SSD storage for data centers, from Intel in 2021.
"While an IPO was expected to ease investment burdens and expand capacity for shareholder returns, the review has been discontinued in light of market conditions and share price trends," SK Hynix said in a release .
Despite the turmoil, all of tech's mega-caps have maintained their investment-grade rating even as they've opened their wallets to fuel their build-outs, including through debt. Even with that group of companies, the market is showing some jitters.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg speaks during the Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, California, Sept. 23, 2026.
Meta saw its stock plunge 7% on Thursday after the company reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter of over $2 billion while raising the floor of its full-year capex to $135 billion from $130 billion. Meta also said it plans to spend about $825 billion over the coming years on various leases and contracts, with over $450 billion of those leases being non-cancellable take-or-pay agreements.
Spreads on Meta's five-year CDS reached all-time highs of over 124 basis points. CDS on Nvidia and Oracle also touched records, with their spreads hitting 126 basis points and 343 basis points, respectively, this week. Oracle's stock has lost over one-third of its value this year, and now the company faces risks of a credit rating downgrade .
John Williams, who leads the derivatives practice at law firm Milbank LLP, says investors are seeking numerous ways beyond buying CDS to hedge their bets with respect to the AI trade.
"There's so much investment going into it that it's just very appropriate to look for risk management tools, completely regardless of whether you're bullish or bearish," Williams said. "It would be crazy for people not to be looking for appropriate risk management tools for it."
Brian Stutland, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, told CNBC's "SquawkBox Asia" last week that it's "all kind of tied together," referring to AI's impact on the whole market.
"Can you drop a bowling ball in one part of the pool and not get any waves downstream to the rest of the Nasdaq?" he said. "I don't know. I have some concern about that."
— CNBC's Katie Tarasov contributed to this report

items.title: North Korea has opened up bridges to Russia and China – in which direction will it go? - The Guardian
items.summary: North Korea has opened up bridges to Russia and China – in which direction will it go?  The Guardian
items.content:
Residents sit at a viewing platform overlooking the newly opened New Yalu River Bridge Photograph: Florence Lo/Reuters
Residents sit at a viewing platform overlooking the newly opened New Yalu River Bridge Photograph: Florence Lo/Reuters
North Korea has opened up bridges to Russia and China – in which direction will it go?
Kim Jong-un has opened the borders to both his key allies in Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, but for different reasons
For more than a decade, local Chinese residents pilloried it as nothing more than an empty bridge that led to a North Korean vegetable patch on the other side.
Fast forward 12 years and dozens of trucks are now traversing the bridge linking China to North Korea, boosting trade for the reclusive regime. But it has also triggered concern that it could intensify a struggle for influence over the North between Beijing and the region’s other major power, Russia.
map The New Yalu River Bridge connects the north-eastern Chinese city of Dandong with Sinuiju in North Korea and has four lanes and stretches 3km (1.9 miles) across the Yalu river. It is expected to ease congestion on the ageing Friendship Bridge nearby.
It opened on 15 October, about a month after another major crossing – this time between North Korea and Russia. The first road bridge across their short shared border , named the Yakov Novichenko Bridge, reportedly made Chinese officials uneasy, coming on top of signs from the North Korean leader Kim Jong-un that he is prioritising ties with Moscow.
map “China’s interest in buttressing its influence in North Korea is certainly reinforced by the diversifying North Korea-Russia relationship — ties that China tolerates but watches closely as they add complexity to its relationship with its provocative neighbour,” says Carla Freeman, director of the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies’ Foreign Policy Institute.
Since late 2024, the North Korean leader has sent ammunition and as many as 16,000 troops to support Vladimir Putin ’s war in Ukraine, and has held two summits with the Russian president in the past three years. In 2024, the leaders signed a mutual defence pact that includes a clause requiring the countries to come to each other’s aid if attacked.
Trucks adorned with Chinese flags cross the newly opened New Yalu River Bridge into North Korea’s Sinuiju.
Photograph: Florence Lo/Reuters In return for arms and combat soldiers, Pyongyang is getting hard currency, real-time battlefield experience for its troops, weapons technology and the opportunity to extend political and economic cooperation beyond its traditional ally China .
North Korea stands to benefit from increased trade but for China, the bridge could be of more geopolitical value than economic given how little trade China does with its neighbour compared with its other partners.
However, the insular regime in Pyongyang is thought to be reluctant to increase its economic dependence on China, by far its biggest trading partner and aid donor, and may still resent Beijing’s previous support for UN sanctions targeting the North’s nuclear weapons programme .
In the past two years, however, Russian and Chinese support for UN sanctions has collapsed. “The main restriction on trade with North Korea is not the infrastructure but international sanctions,” says Justin Hastings, a professor of international relations and comparative politics at Sydney University. “However, because China’s enforcement of UN sanctions has become desultory and Russia has actively repudiated their enforcement, North Korea is in a position to benefit from increased trade and weapons help (at least from Russia).”
The newly opened New Yalu River Bridge could be of more geopolitical importance than economic for China. Photograph: Florence Lo/Reuters The North’s “open” border with China contrasts dramatically with the one it shares with South Korea. In 2024, the North said it would sever all rail and road links with its neighbour, months after Kim said he would abandon the goal of peaceful reunification and declared South Korea his country’s “ principal enemy ”.
But Fyodor Tertitskiy, a North Korea expert at Korea University in Seoul, believes neither China nor Russia can influence North Korea in any meaningful way, citing Kim’s refusal to surrender his nuclear weapons or moderate his iron grip on power – two changes that would be welcomed in Moscow and Beijing.
“Both countries understand that Kim Jong-un would rather accept a complete breakdown in relationships than submit,” he says. “So I doubt we are seeing a straightforward struggle for influence. Kim is trying to play the two against each other, but China and Russia are not rivals like the Soviet Union and China were in the 1970s.”
Kim is more likely to turn to China improve his country’s struggling economy, while Beijing is eager to revive its role as the North’s biggest influence, according to Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul.
“After expanding military cooperation with Russia … Kim Jong-un is leveraging his windfall from Moscow for additional gains from Beijing. China may seek to recover lost influence by increasing trade and people-to-people exchanges, but the Kim regime prizes autonomy and wants to limit foreign ideological and cultural influences.”
The South Korean government said last year that at least 17 active road and rail links connect North Korea and China along their 1,400 km-long border.
Beijing is eager to revive its role as the North’s biggest influence. Photograph: Florence Lo/Reuters Tertitskiy is “not particularly optimistic” that the increased contact the bridges will bring means improvements to the lives of ordinary North Koreans or lead to a more western-style economy. “I think it will make reform even less likely. Why pursue reforms and take risks when you can just get what you need from abroad?”
Analysts say the expected rise in trade across the Yalu bridge is likely to be modest at first. But it could become a bellwether for the state of Sino-North Korean ties, says Easley.
“China remains economically indispensable to North Korea in ways that Russia cannot replace,” he says, adding, “In that sense, the bridge may offer an inadvertent window into bilateral relations if flows are visibly interrupted in the future.”

items.title: Google’s $250 Billion AI Chip Opportunity Takes Aim at Nvidia - I/O Fund
items.summary: Google’s $250 Billion AI Chip Opportunity Takes Aim at Nvidia  I/O Fund
items.content:
In April, there was a major shift in the AI accelerator market, and for once, it didn’t come from Nvidia. Six months later, merchant TPUs are moving from announcement to commercial execution, with Google recognizing its first revenue from TPU systems in Q2 (from a small base). Last quarter, Cloud revenue growth accelerated to 82% for $24.8 billion, compared to $22.5 billion expected. In addition, new details around the TPU 8t show that Google’s threat to Nvidia is not limited to inference.
At the time, we pointed out that Google may be one of Nvidia’s strongest AI challengers , as Big Tech is closest to the problems that accelerators must solve. The problem that Google is prioritizing is lower cost per token, with token economics becoming a predominant concern as AI spending is pushing Big Tech’s free cash flows into the red.
Below, we discuss two reasons why Google’s AI story is about to change, not from advancements in AI software, but by going after one of the most profitable hardware businesses the tech industry has ever seen.
Two Financial Benefits to Custom Silicon and What TPU 8i Aims to Achieve
With Google reporting Q3 earnings next week, its TPU strategy could become a central focus of the earnings call, as merchant custom silicon addresses two major investor concerns. First, by lowering its cost per token, each dollar of capex stretches further. Secondly, selling TPUs to third-party customers creates an additional revenue stream for Google outside of monetizing capacity via cloud rentals.
Google’s newest TPU 8t and 8i both claim significant performance-per-dollar improvements over the prior generation, TPU v7 (Ironwood). This stems from increased HBM bandwidth , with 8t and 8i packing 216GB and 288GB respectively, up from Ironwood’s 192GB, as well as increased scale-up bandwidth, with 8i doubling Ironwood’s to 19.2 Tb/s.
With the TPU 8i, Google is addressing the problem of high costs (and consequently weak cash flows) through coherent shared memory, which plays a critical role in improving inference efficiency.
Arguably, the most critical point to understand about Google’s design advantage with the 8i is that the 331.8 TB of memory is shared across the entire pod over Google’s inter-chip interconnect (ICI). In our previous article, Google TPU v8 vs Nvidia: How Inference is Rewriting the AI Market we discussed that SRAM capacity and Boardfly topology also contribute to latency improvements.
Per our article, “Google noted that TPU 8i delivers up to an 80% performance-per-dollar improvement over the Ironwood TPU, particularly at low-latency targets for large MoE models.” This performance gain is not limited to 8i, as 8t offers up to 2.7X better performance-per-dollar on training.
To put this in different terms, this will allow customers to serve almost twice the volume at the same cost.

The report is built on the same investment discipline that drove our YTD outperformance and surfaced some of the biggest AI winners of 2026.
TPUs Help Gemini Deliver Competitive Cost per Intelligence Tasks
The benefit from this improved performance-per-dollar is evident in lower token costs, where Google offers among the lowest “cost per intelligence task.”
According to Artificial Analysis, cost per intelligence task reflects average prices for real-world evaluation scenarios, rather than just a simple per-million token price via APIs. In the evaluations, Gemini ranked among the lowest cost per intelligence compared to leading models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta.
For example, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview costs an average of $1.30, or 51% cheaper than GPT 5.5 (high) and 76% cheaper than Claude Sonnet 5.5. However, lightweight models such as GPT 6 Luna provide stiffer cost competition, with an average cost of $0.07 versus Gemini 3.8 Flash Lite’s $0.19.
Claude models rank as the most expensive to run, occupying the four highest-cost positions. Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview averages $1.30 per intelligence task versus $5.46 for Claude Sonnet 5.5 and $7.63 for Claude Fable 5.1. The 8i’s deployment would compound the already significant serving cost reductions Google achieved in 2025. Last Q4, Google’s CEO stated there was a 78% reduction in Gemini serving unit costs throughout 2025, with this occurring prior to the optimized v8 generation and the significant performance improvements it delivers.
As inference workloads shift from Ironwood to the new generation, that 80% reduction in performance-per-dollar can allow Google to continue lowering serving costs and help broaden Gemini adoption.
Third-Party TPU Sales Could Become Google’s Next Major Revenue Driver
Second, selling TPUs to third-party customers creates an additional revenue stream for Google outside of monetizing capacity via rentals. Google first made the shift to selling TPUs to third-party customers in April, recognizing the first TPU-related revenue in Q2 at a small scale.
Despite being quite early in this endeavor, its TPU customer list is notable. According to Broadcom’s update in Q3, Anthropic is deploying 1GW of Ironwood TPUs in 2026 , 5GWs of TPU 8i in 2027 and an incremental 10GW in 2028.
Meta signed a multibillion-dollar TPU deal in February and was rumored to explore third-party TPU deployments, while Google’s joint venture with Blackstone aims to bring its first 0.5 GW of TPU capacity online in 2027.
This rapid multi-GW ramp is expected to create a significant revenue stream for Google, with the majority of shipments starting to land in 2027 and beyond. Barclays projects third-party TPU sales could generate roughly $20 billion in revenue in 2026, more than triple to $67 billion in 2027 and more than triple again to $252.7 billion by 2028. This is one of the most aggressive ramps expected, with Piper Sandler and Morgan Stanley projecting just over $100 billion by 2028.
To put this in perspective, that 2028 projection from Barclays would imply that third-party TPU sales would ramp to the current run rate of Google’s Search business in just two and a half years.
Analysts project rapid growth in Google’s third-party TPU business through 2028. Barclays forecasts TPU sales reaching $252.7 billion by 2028, while Piper Sandler and Morgan Stanley estimate approximately $104 billion and $108 billion, respectively. However, this secondary revenue stream currently comes with a fair degree of risk. At the moment, Anthropic accounts for the majority of expected third-party shipments, creating customer concentration and financing risk for TPU shipments.
Merchant TPU Sales Shift the Capex Burden to Customers
This secondary revenue stream from selling TPUs also shifts the capex burden away from Google to its third-party customers. With $200 billion earmarked towards capex this year, any incremental revenue that doesn’t require Google to build the data center first is unusually valuable.
For Google to deploy TPUs through Google Cloud and rent them to customers, it must first pay upfront for the data center, the power, the cooling and the chips, reflected in its 2026 capex bill at $195-205 billion. Once TPUs are installed and energized, Google can then recover its capex by renting these chips out in the cloud across several years.
However, merchant TPU sales to third-party customers flip that equation around. Under this sales model, customers would fund the data center and the hardware purchases, with Google’s revenue coming at chip delivery instead of those multi-year rental terms. Thus, that estimated $253 billion revenue stream would appear in financials as systems are shipped.
One major drawback to shifting capex to its customers is that R&D labs such as Anthropic, who accounts for the majority of projected shipments, do not enjoy the same balance sheet strength as hyperscalers. While Anthropic says it was cash flow positive in Q3, it does not have the same strength in terms of cash as the hyperscalers do. If Google plays a larger role in helping finance chip purchases (where Broadcom currently is active with its AI XPV platform), some of the cash benefit shifts back onto Google’s balance sheet or into contingent obligations.

One caveat to external TPU revenue is that it could weigh on Google’s margins, as TPU system sales will carry a far lower margin than cloud revenue.
For context, Google Cloud reported an operating margin of 35.6% as of Q2, expanding roughly 15 points YoY as operating income more than tripled to $8.8 billion as AI services ramped.
However, by shifting to selling full TPU racks, revenue will now include HBM, networking components, cooling and power, much of which will pass through at little markup. Broadcom offers a clear example for this, noting that as “TPUs continue to accelerate, there’ll be pressure overall on margins” as these lower-margin systems contribute a higher proportion of AI semiconductor revenue.

The report is built on the same investment discipline that drove our YTD outperformance and surfaced some of the biggest AI winners of 2026.
For Google, margin impacts could be more pronounced, as it’s expected that third-party TPU sales will carry far lower margins than even what Broadcom realizes. Even with the higher mix of lower-margin XPU projects, Broadcom is maintaining a mid-70% gross margin, though Morgan Stanley estimates that Google’s third-party TPU sales could carry a gross margin of just 30%.
Impacts in the near-term are likely to be relatively minimal as TPU revenue should be easily absorbed by its broader cloud suite, but come later in 2027 and especially 2028, the higher mix of TPU-driven revenue (potentially outpacing broader Cloud services) could weigh on segment margins.
Google’s Challenge to Nvidia Extends Beyond Inference
While the 8i targets inference workloads, new details on the training-focused TPU 8t show how far Google is pushing scale.
At Hot Chips in August, Google outlined an 8t ‘superpod’ of 9,600 chips with access to 2PB of shared HBM and 121 exaflops of FP4 compute, offering roughly twice the performance-per-watt of Ironwood. The scale is made possible by Google’s optical circuit switches, which can dynamically carve slices out of a 9,600-chip pod. Compare this to Nvidia’s current rack-scale systems, where the scale-up domain tops out at 72 GPUs.
Google is also taking this scale a step further with the introduction of its dedicated Virgo Network fabric. With Virgo, Google can link together fourteen of the ‘superpods’ in a single fabric, capable of supporting 134,400 TPUs in a single domain with 47 PB/s of bandwidth. This cluster size offers 1.6 yottaflops of compute (or 1.6 million exaflops) for massive, large-scale frontier model training.
According to AMD at CES 2026, “Reaching yottascale AI compute would require the equivalent of millions of today’s Frontier exaflop-class supercomputers operating together.”
Nvidia Delay Could Help Google; But it’s Not Necessary
As we’ve said in the past, Nvidia’s product roadmap has consistently pushed the limits across the supply chain. This led to a delay in 2024 on Blackwell, due to the systems overheating.
In May, we discussed a reported one-quarter delay in Nvidia’s Rubin ramp, stating:
“Lastly, the reported one-quarter delay of Nvidia’s Rubin ramp, officially scheduled for Q3 2026, could offer a strong argument for diversification across AI accelerators. Notably, TrendForce revised its estimate of Rubin’s contribution to Nvidia’s total high-end GPU shipments for 2026 down from 29% to 22% to account for such a delay.
Factors contributing to the reported delay and TrendForce’s revision include “the time required to validate the newer HBM4 memory used by the chips, challenges with the migration to Nvidia’s faster ConnectX-9 NICs, the system’s higher overall power consumption, and the more advanced liquid cooling requirements.”
Since then, another report has surfaced. In July, CNBC reported that SemiAnalysis found Nvidia’s Kyber rack architecture had been delayed by more than 12 months to 2028, citing a PCB midplane manufacturing issue, though Nvidia has publicly disputed the report.
If these reports prove accurate on the Kyber rack delay, or even if Nvidia shifts the Rubin Ultra architecture from its original planned four-die design to a “2+2” design as rumored, the impacts would be larger than just timing. Kyber marks the system that expands Nvidia’s scale-up domain from 72 GPUs to 576 GPU dies per rack.
A delay to 2028 would mean Nvidia’s largest coherent domain stays in the 72-GPU class through 2027, the same year Google’s merchant TPU revenue is set to ramp with pods of 1,152 chips for inference and 9,600 chips for training (slightly larger than the 9,216-chip pod with Ironwood).
Google is also quickly catching up to Nvidia in terms of unit volume, although a majority of these will be used internally to serve Gemini. However, any potential delay on Nvidia’s roadmap could open the door for further market share gains, as estimated TPU volumes range from 8.8 to 10 million in 2027, above UBS’ estimate for 8.8 million Rubin chips next year.
HBM Supply Constraints Remain the Largest Bottleneck
HBM is the leading constraint the AI industry faces, and commentary from industry executives suggests that the shortage is only worsening with little relief expected in 2027 or even 2028.
In our recent newsletter, Why Nvidia’s SK Hynix Deal Leaves Little AI Memory Supply , we explained that based on industry estimates, Nvidia and Alphabet are expected to demand roughly three-quarters of global HBM supply in 2027. When factoring in AMD’s Helios ramp and numerous custom silicon projects at other hyperscalers, there is little chance for meaningful HBM supply relief or allocation increase.
Faced with such tight supply constraints, even Nvidia, the largest buyer, is paying up to secure access to HBM, and Google likely is having to do the same given its allocation is nearly on par with Nvidia’s, and far ahead of AMD’s.
With the memory market recently shifting in favor of long-term agreements with substantial prepayments, it means cash goes out the door long before TPU revenue is recognized. Customer deposits for third-party TPU capacity can offset this, but it’s a timing drag during a ramp, which is exactly what 2027 will be.
Google’s greatest competitive advantage may not be building a faster chip than Nvidia, but rather in building AI infrastructure at a lower cost. The company has spent years designing accelerators around the demands of its own AI workloads, giving it an advantage that traditional chip companies cannot easily replace.
Selling TPUs to third-party customers opens up a new revenue stream for Google, with analysts forecasting a wide range of revenue from $100 billion to $250 billion as soon as 2028. The higher-end of those forecasts represents what took Search decades to achieve.
The one caveat? HBM constraints and customer financing could limit how quickly the sales translate to improved cash flow. Read more here .

European Natural Gas Prices Surge to Highest Level Since 2022
The benchmark European natural gas price jumped by 3% at opening in Amsterdam on Friday as the Middle East escalation continues to restrict Qatari LNG flows and some EU countries started tapping gas in storage as temperatures drop.
The front-month price at the Dutch Title Transfer Facility (TTF) , the benchmark for Europe's gas trading, jumped by 3% at 7 a.m. Amsterdam time on Friday, as oil prices also rose, and Brent hit a five-month high of $114 per barrel as concerns grow that Houthi attacks could hit Saudi Arabian energy facilities.
At $103.40 (92.30 euros) per megawatt-hour (MWh), the European gas price is now at its highest levels since December 2022, when Europe faced the first winter without most of the Russian pipeline gas supply. The current price is also equivalent to over $30 per million British thermal units (MMBtu).
"European gas prices also remain extremely sensitive to developments in the Persian Gulf, with LNG flows increasingly likely to be largely absent from the market for at least much of the Northern Hemisphere winter," ING's commodities strategists Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey wrote in a note early on Friday.
TTF rallied 3% on Thursday, settling above 90 euros per MWh, its highest since December 2022. On Friday morning, the TTF benchmark price topped 92 euros per MWh as the heating season approaches, Europe is still deprived of Qatari LNG, and storage sites are only 75% full, which is over 10 percentage points lower than the five-year average.
EU storage sites were only 74.62% full as of October 22, per data from Gas Infrastructure Europe. That's well below the five-year average of about 86% for this time of the year so close to the start of the heating season.
"EU gas storage also appears to have peaked at just under 75% full," ING's strategists said today.
