Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, October 23, 2026
Ukrainian officials are widely reporting continued in-motion speed restrictions on SpaceX’s low-earth orbit satellite communication technology (Starlink and Starshield) on October 23, but the situation remains unclear. Ukrainian sources, including the Ukrainian General Staff and sources within the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense (MoD), reported on October 23 that Ukrainian forces have observed “cases of connection loss” in Starlink/Starshield terminal operations at speeds of 161 kilometers per hour (around 100 miles per hour).[1] Sources within the Ukrainian MoD stated that there has been “no confirmation” about the removal of in-motion speed restrictions.[2] Ukrainian defense minister Serhii Sternenko stated that the situation with Starlink/Starshield speed restrictions “remains ambiguous” since some Ukrainian units report the resumption of operations at speeds exceeding the previously established limits, but the resumption does not apply to all missions, and he noted that some disruptions continue.[3] The situation regarding in-motion Starlink/Starshield speed restrictions remains unclear, but Ukrainian sources are emphasizing that Ukrainian forces continue experiencing problems with accessing Starlink/Starshield terminals as of October 23.
Russia and Ukraine have reportedly agreed to a limited ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky, Kherson Oblast. The White House reported on October 23 that US First Lady Melania Trump secured a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in Russia-occupied Oleshky, Kherson Oblast beginning on October 29 to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries and a civilian evacuation from the city amid a dire humanitarian crisis.[4] Ukraine’s Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets confirmed on October 23 the White House’s press release and noted that Ukraine and Russia agreed to conduct a humanitarian mission in occupied Oleshky, including securing a limited ceasefire, delivering humanitarian cargo to the city, and ensuring the free movement of civilians from the settlement.[5] Russian Chief of the General Staff Army General Valery Gerasimov confirmed on October 23 that Russia agreed to the limited ceasefire in the Kherson direction beginning at 0400 local Moscow time on October 27 — a notably different start date from the one given in the White House press release.[6]
Russian occupation authorities are fully responsible for the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky and have repeatedly and deliberately blocked evacuation and humanitarian routes into the settlement since the beginning of Russia's occupation.[7] Russian occupation authorities stopped the delivery of food and other critical supplies into Oleshky in late December 2025 and have failed to deliver any food or medicine to Oleshky since May 2026. The Kremlin rejected three local humanitarian ceasefire proposals from Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets in May, July, and September 2026, after which Ukrainian forces conducted an operation to provide food to Oleshky residents via drone drops in September 2026.[8] Russian authorities have long refused to address the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky, and Gerasimov’s October 23 statement is the first instance of a Russian attempt to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries.
Russian President Vladimir Putin articulated his long-standing commitment to wider territorial aims in Ukraine far beyond Donetsk Oblast by invoking mythologized and false Russian “historical claims”. Putin claimed on October 22 that occupied Ukraine is “the territory of historical Russia” while rejecting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s October 21 proposal to freeze the current frontline as part of a ceasefire agreement.[9] Putin also claimed that the “latest genetic research” identifies Russians and Ukrainians as “one people.” Putin’s October 22 reference to “historical Russia” likely refers to "Novorossiya" — an amorphous invented region in southern and eastern Ukraine that the Kremlin has claimed is “integral” to Russia.[10] Novorossiya notably includes not only Crimea and the four oblasts that Russia has illegally annexed (Luhansk, Donetsk, Zaporizhia, and Kherson oblasts), but also Kharkiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Mykolaiv, and Odesa oblasts.[11] Putin’s invocation of Russia’s historical claims demands that Ukraine surrender the Ukrainian-controlled 20.5 percent of Donetsk Oblast, 24.5 percent of Zaporizhia Oblast, including Zaporizhzhia City with a pre-war population of over 700,000 people, and 30 percent of Kherson Oblast, including Kherson City with a pre-war population of nearly 300,000 people. Putin’s October 23 statement explicitly demonstrates that Russian demands extend far beyond Ukraine’s Fortress Belt and Donetsk Oblast and may include the entire territory of Ukraine . Putin also emphasized his commitment to achieving all Russian war goals, which include the Russian demand for Ukraine’s full capitulation.[12] Putin’s statement demonstrates that the Kremlin is willing to participate in “negotiations” with Ukraine solely for the purpose of accepting Kyiv's surrender — not for the purpose of coming to some compromise peace agreement.
Putin also agreed to discuss the “European security architecture as a whole” after ensuring Ukraine’s and Russia’s future security.[13] Putin’s comment on “revising” the European security architecture refers to another Russian long-standing demand first articulated in the December 2021 ultimatum preceding the full-scale invasion that includes halting the deployment of military forces and weapons systems to NATO states that joined the alliance after 1997 and granting Russia a veto over certain NATO exercises.[14] Putin’s December 2021 demands are incompatible with US President Donald Trump’s commitment to maintaining a US military presence in Poland and the current US troop deployments in the Baltic States.
The Kremlin appears to be increasingly adopting a more cautious monetary policy amid continued inflationary pressures, which may pose risks to wage growth and Russia’s defense industrial base (DIB). The Russian Central Bank announced on October 23 that it would keep the key interest rate at 14 percent for the second consecutive month, after lowering the rate 10 times over the past 18 months, citing elevated price pressure and high inflation expectations.[15] The Central Bank’s baseline scenario assumes an average key interest rate of 12.5 to 13.5 percent in 2027 — only 0.5 to 1.5 percentage points below the current rate. The Central Bank noted that underlying price growth is “not slowing” and identified pro-inflationary risks (or risk factors that increase inflation over the medium term), including price growth between five and six percent and estimated annual inflation of 6.8 percent. The Central Bank estimated that annual inflation will range between 7.1 and 7.6 percent by the end of 2026, a slight increase from the Central Bank’s September 11 announcement, and noted that volatile items like motor fuel (an oblique reference to the effects of Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure) will continue impacting price dynamics. Russian Central Bank Chairwoman Elvira Nabiullina stated on October 23 that supply and demand continue facing inflationary risks, elevated inflation expectations, labor market tensions, and a larger budget deficit.[16] Nabiullina stated that Russia has experienced a decrease in consumer activity and that Russia’s GDP growth estimates for 2026 are between 0.5 and one percent. Nabiullina stated that the Central Bank is aiming to return the inflation rate to four percent in 2027.
The Russian Central Bank’s continued reduction of the key interest rate over an 18-month period prior to September 2026 likely contributed to domestic inflationary pressures.[17] Nabiullina has consistently expressed the need for monetary restraint — often trying to resist the Kremlin’s demands to expand capital availability for the Russian DIB and devalue the ruble to increase export revenues, despite ongoing fiscal inflationary pressures.[18] The Central Bank’s apparent success in avoiding further interest rate reductions at this time indicates that Putin has likely become more tolerant of contractionary monetary policy. Putin has recently prioritized reducing inflation to secure support amongst the Russian population by attempting to reduce the economic effects of Russian war spending, a prioritization that may have led him to accept Nabiullina’s fiscal policy for now.[19] Keeping the key rate at the current level will likely suppress wage growth and limit the amount of capital available to the Russian DIB, which may prevent Putin from achieving his goals of raising Russians’ effective purchasing power and maintaining the DIB’s production capacity. It remains difficult to assess, however, what effect fiscal policy will have on wage inflation and Russians’ quality of life, since Russia’s persistent labor shortages drive wage inflation for employed individuals while households face pressures that nominal wage figures do not capture.[20]
A likely Russian drone struck a cargo ship off the coast of Romania and drone debris fell in Moldova on October 23. Romanian President Nicusor Dan stated on October 23 that an unspecified drone struck a Comoros-flagged Khoryv cargo ship “near Romanian territorial waters” and added that the strike is a consequence of “Russia’s aggression against Ukraine.”[21] The Romanian Naval Authority reported that the Khoryv vessel sent a distress signal about 13 nautical miles (around 24 kilometers and just outside of the Romanian territorial waters) off the coast of Constanta, Romania.[22] European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the October 23 drone strike yet another “Russian escalation” in the Black Sea.[23] Territorial waters extend up to 12 nautical miles (about 22 kilometers) from the country's shoreline, and states have sovereignty and jurisdiction over their territorial waters.[24] The October 23 drone strike comes against the backdrop of recent escalating Russian strikes against vessels in the Black Sea, including likely Russian drone strikes against two commercial tankers within Romanian territorial waters on October 14 and 15 and strikes against civilian vessels in the Bulgarian Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) overnight on October 12 to 13.[25] The Moldovan police separately reported on October 23 that drone debris fell up to 100 meters from a residential building near Chistelnica, Telenesti Raion, Moldova.[26] These continuous, likely Russian violations of Moldovan and Romanian sovereign territory demonstrate Russia’s increasing willingness to pursue strike tactics that may directly impact the territory of NATO or NATO-aligned states.[27]
Ukraine and Russia conducted civilian prisoner and prisoner of war (POW) exchanges on October 23. Ukrainian and Russian authorities reported on October 23 that Ukraine and Russia exchanged 270 prisoners each.[28] Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reported that Russia returned nine civilian prisoners back to Ukraine as part of the exchange.[29] Ukrainian Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of POWs reported that the October 23 POW exchange is the third stage of a combined prisoner swap that began on August 19, 2026.[30] Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets separately reported that Russia and Ukraine exchanged seven more civilians on October 23.[31]
Ukrainian officials are widely reporting continued in-motion speed restrictions on SpaceX’s low-earth orbit satellite communication technology (Starlink and Starshield) on October 23, but the situation remains unclear.

Russian President Vladimir Putin articulated his long-standing commitment to wider territorial aims in Ukraine far beyond Donetsk Oblast by invoking mythologized and false Russian “historical claims”.
The Kremlin appears to be increasingly adopting a more cautious monetary policy amid continued inflationary pressures, which may pose risks to wage growth and Russia’s defense industrial base (DIB).
A likely Russian drone struck a cargo ship off the coast of Romania, and drone debris fell in Moldova on October 23.
Ukraine and Russia conducted civilian prisoner and prisoner of war (POW) exchanges on October 23.
Ukrainian forces recently advanced west of Kostyantynivka.
Russian forces launched 176 drones against Ukraine overnight. Ukraine continued its long-range strike campaign against Russian military assets overnight on October 22 to 23 and on October 23.
We do not report in detail on Russian war crimes because these activities are well-covered in Western media and do not directly affect the military operations we are assessing and forecasting. We will continue to evaluate and report on the effects of these criminal activities on the Ukrainian military and the Ukrainian population and specifically on combat in Ukrainian urban areas. We utterly condemn Russian violations of the laws of armed conflict and the Geneva Conventions and crimes against humanity even though we do not describe them in these reports.
Ukrainian forces launched a large strike package toward Moscow City, prompting the suspension of operations at all four Moscow area airports and the evacuation of government administrative buildings. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin claimed on October 23 that 155 Ukrainian drones targeted Moscow Oblast overnight on October 22 and 23.[32] Russian state aviation regulator Rosaviatsia announced on October 23 that Vnukovo, Domodedovo, Zhukovsky, and Sheremetyevo airports — all four major airports servicing Moscow City — introduced temporary restrictions.[33] A Ukrainian open-source intelligence (OSINT) channel posted an image on October 23 showing drone debris on the tarmac at Sheremetyevo Airport.[34] The channel also published footage on October 23 purporting to show balloons flying over Moscow City, purportedly carrying explosives or small drones.[35] Russian opposition outlet Astra reported on October 23 that Russian authorities evacuated the IQ-Quarter tower in Moscow City, which reportedly houses offices for the Russian Ministries of Economic Development, the Ministry of Industry and Trade, the Ministry of Digital Development, and the Federal Agency for Technical Regulation and Metrology.[36]
Ukrainian forces conducted a series of long-range strikes against a Russian defense industrial facility, a chemical production plant, and administrative and military infrastructure in Russia. Geolocated footage published on October 23 shows the moment of a likely Ukrainian missile strike against the Proton plant in Oryol City, Oryol Oblast (roughly 161 kilometers from the frontline).[37] A Ukrainian OSINT channel stated that reportedly Ukrainian Storm Shadow cruise missiles struck the plant.[38] Ukrainian defense source Militarnyi reported that the plant manufactures components for the Russian S-71 Kover cruise missiles, Iskander-M ballistic missiles, and Pantsir-S1 air defense systems.[39] Geolocated footage published on October 23 shows a Ukrainian FP-1 drone approaching the Azot UralKhim Chemical Plant in Berezniki, Perm Krai (roughly 1,585 kilometers from the international border) and smoke plumes rising from the facility.[40] Perm Krai governor Dmitry Makhonin acknowledged on October 23 that Ukrainian forces struck and damaged an industrial facility.[41] A Ukrainian OSINT channel posted footage on October 23 purporting to show Ukrainian forces striking a Russian Federal Taxation Service data center in Gorodets, Nizhny Novgorod Oblast (roughly 785 kilometers from the international border).[42] Nizhny Novgorod Oblast Governor Gleb Nikitin acknowledged on October 23 that drone debris damaged unspecified infrastructure in Gorodets raion.[43] A Ukrainian OSINT channel posted on October 23 an image showing smoke plumes near Baltimore Air Base in Voronezh City (roughly 190 kilometers from the international border).[44] The channel reported that preliminary information indicates that Ukrainian forces targeted the former Voronezh Military Aviation Engineering University and an adjacent military aircraft parking area.[45] Voronezh Oblast Governor Alexander Gusev acknowledged on October 23 that Ukrainian drones targeted Voronezh City.[46]
Russian objective: Create defensible buffer zones in Sumy Oblast along the international border
Russian forces continued limited offensive operations in northern Sumy Oblast on October 23 but did not advance.[47]
Russian objective: Push Ukrainian forces back from the international border to create a defensible buffer zone with Belgorod Oblast and approach Kharkiv City
Russian forces recently conducted infiltration missions northeast and northwest of Kharkiv City. Ukrainian forces struck Russian positions southeast of Khrypuny (northeast of Kharkiv City) and south of Nova Kozacha (northwest of Kharkiv City), according to geolocated footage published on October 20 and 22, respectively, after what ISW assesses were Russian infiltration missions.[48]
Russian forces continued offensive operations northeast of Velykyi Burluk on October 22 and 23 but did not advance.[49]
Russian objective: Cross the Oskil River in Kharkiv Oblast and push westward into eastern Kharkiv Oblast and northern Donetsk Oblas t
Russian forces continued offensive operations in the Kupyansk direction on October 22 and 23 but did not make confirmed advances.[50]
Neither Russian nor Ukrainian sources reported ground activity in the Borova direction on October 23.
Russian Main Effort: Capture Ukraine's Fortress Belt and complete the seizure of Donetsk Oblast
Russian Subordinate Main Effort #1 – Encircle the Fortress Belt from the northwest
Russian objective: Seize Lyman and cross the Siverskyi Donets River to support a wide encirclement of the Fortress Belt – assessed objective of the Russian 25th Combined Arms Army and Western Grouping of Forces elements
Russian forces continued offensive operations in the Lyman direction on October 22 and 23 but did not advance.[51] A Russian milblogger claimed on October 23 that Russian forces are developing an offensive from Yampil (southeast of Lyman) towards Ozerne (southwest of Yampil) and Dibrova (west of Yampil).[52]
Russian Subordinate Main Effort #2 – Advance on the Fortress Belt from the east
Russian objective: Advance on Slovyansk, Kramatorsk, and Druzhkivka from the east – assessed objective of the Russian 3rd Combined Arms Army and Southern Grouping of Forces elements
Russian forces continued limited offensive operations east of Slovyansk on October 23.[53] Donetsk Oblast Military Administration Head Vadym Filashkin ordered on October 22 the mandatory evacuation of all families with children in Kramatorsk and Slovyansk hromadas due to ongoing Russian strikes against civilian and residential infrastructure.[54]
Russian Subordinate Main Effort #3 – Advance on the Fortress Belt from the south
Russian objective: Advance on Kostyantynivka and Druzhkivka from the south and southwest, east of the Kazenyi Torets River – assessed objective of the Russian 8th Combined Arms Army and Southern Grouping of Forces elements
Ukrainian forces recently advanced west of Kostyantynivka. Ukrainian forces recently advanced in northern Sofiivka, according to geolocated footage published on October 22.[55]
Russian Subordinate Main Effort #4 – Encircle the Fortress Belt from the southwest
Russian objective: Conduct a wide encirclement of the Fortress Belt from near Dobropillya and Pokrovsk west of the Kazenyi Torets River – assessed objective of the Russian 51st Combined Arms Army and Central Grouping of Forces elements
Russian forces recently conducted an infiltration mission in southern Dobropillya. Russian forces are operating in southern Dobropillya, according to geolocated footage published on October 22, after what ISW assesses was a Russian infiltration mission.[56] Ukrainian military observer Kostyantyn Mashovets reported on October 21 that Russian forces infiltrated southern Dobropillya.[57]
Russian sources continue to use likely AI-generated or AI-altered footage to make aggrandized claims in the Dobropillya direction. A Russian source published footage on October 23 purportedly showing Russian forces raising flags in Vesele Pole (north of Dobropillya and roughly 12 kilometers from the furthest assessed extent of Russian advances).[58] ISW has reason to believe that the Russian flag raising video may be AI-generated or AI-altered, which would be consistent with previous Russian information operations that use AI footage to claim battlefield advances.[59]
Russian Supporting Effort: Advance into Dnipropetrovsk Oblast
Russian objective: Interdict Ukrainian ground lines of communication that support Ukrainian positions in Donetsk Oblast and envelop Ukrainian positions in southwestern Donetsk Oblast – assessed objective of elements of the Russian Central and Eastern groupings of forces
Neither Russian nor Ukrainian sources reported ground activity in the Novopavlivka and Oleksandrivka directions on October 23.
Russian objective: Maintain frontline positions, secure rear areas against Ukrainian strikes, and advance within tube artillery range of Zaporizhzhia City – assessed objective of the Russian Eastern and Dnepr Grouping of Forces
Russian forces continued offensive operations in the Hulyaipole direction on October 22 and 23 but did not advance as Ukrainian forces counterattacked in the area.[60]
Russian forces recently conducted infiltration missions west of Orikhiv. Ukrainian forces struck Russian positions in eastern Stepnohirsk, according to geolocated footage published on October 22, after what ISW assesses were Russian infiltration missions.[61] A Russian milblogger claimed on October 23 that Russian forces advanced south of Lukyanivske (west of Orikhiv).[62]
Ukrainian forces continued their intermediate-range strike campaign against Russian drone operators in occupied Zaporizhia Oblast. The Ukrainian General Staff reported that Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Rubikon Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies manpower concentration near Kamyanka, Zaporizhia Oblast (roughly 31 kilometers from the frontline) on October 22 or overnight on October 22 to 23.[63]
Neither Russian nor Ukrainian sources reported ground activity in the Kherson direction on October 23.

items.title: Iran has "increased efforts to target U.S. personnel," intel chief warns - CBS News
items.summary: Iran has "increased efforts to target U.S. personnel," intel chief warns  CBS News
items.content:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Friday that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.
The warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, comes as the State Department adjusts staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East , and the U.S. military pares back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen.
"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote.
The memo, which was issued as the Trump administration weighs resuming military strikes against Iran, does not identify specific targets or countries where the alleged plots are underway, or indicate whether attacks may be imminent.
Clayton said the U.S. intelligence community is working to downgrade sensitive intelligence — received through various channels — so it can be shared more broadly with State Department personnel. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was copied on the memo.
The warning follows a series of precautions at U.S. diplomatic facilities across the region. Earlier this week, the State Department ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia. Several other American embassies in the region adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, which allows them to reduce the number of personnel without formally going on ordered departure, CBS News previously reported.
"When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," a U.S. official told CBS News on Friday. "The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."
A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official also told CBS News this week that the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats.
Houthi militants have stepped up drone and missile attacks against Saudi Arabia, targeting oil infrastructure and airports. One strike on Riyadh's King Khalid Airport earlier this month killed at least a dozen people , including a U.S. citizen, and injured hundreds more.
Last weekend, U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other countries warned Americans to exercise caution due to Houthi attacks.
Although the U.S. and Iran have refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, President Trump has not ruled out restarting hostilities after next month's midterm elections. Iran has also continued to take responsibility for attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.
At a campaign rally in Florida on Friday, Mr. Trump suggested the U.S. could launch another operation against Iran if Tehran failed to reach an agreement.
"We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," the president said, invoking the name of the U.S. military campaign launched in February.

items.title: US intelligence warns of advanced Iranian assassination plots - The Jerusalem Post
items.summary: US intelligence warns of advanced Iranian assassination plots  The Jerusalem Post
items.content:
Rubio received intel warning of Iranian plots against US diplomats, official confirms to ‘Post’
The confirmation follows an Axios report revealing a US intelligence warning that Iran has significantly escalated efforts to target American personnel in the Middle East and beyond.
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks to the media after meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, in New York, US, September 23, 2026.
A US official confirmed to The Jerusalem Post on Friday that US Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio received an intelligence memorandum warning that Iran has significantly increased its efforts to target American officials and citizens, with plots to carry out lethal attacks reaching advanced stages.
The confirmation follows a report by Axios , which obtained the October 23 memorandum sent to Rubio by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, with a copy to CIA Director John Ratcliffe.
According to the document, US intelligence agencies have received information through multiple channels indicating that Iran has substantially intensified its efforts to target American personnel.
“The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries,” Clayton wrote.
The intelligence chief warned that information concerning Iranian plots to target American government personnel was relevant to a wider group of individuals than those currently authorized to receive it.
The US Embassy headquarters in Abu Dhabi is pictured on March 3, 2026. (credit: Ryan Lim / AFP via Getty Images)
Clayton said the underlying intelligence had already been shared with appropriately cleared senior members of Rubio’s team and offered to provide the secretary with an additional briefing.
He also pledged to make every effort to downgrade the classification of as much intelligence as possible, allowing Rubio to share the information more broadly with State Department personnel who could potentially be at risk.
The memorandum, marked unclassified, did not identify specific targets, attack methods, or countries outside the Middle East where the alleged plots were being developed.
US reduces diplomatic presence amid regional tensions
The warning comes as the State Department moves to reduce its diplomatic presence across several Middle Eastern countries, amid concerns about Iranian retaliation and the possibility of renewed US military operations against Tehran.
Earlier this week, Washington ordered nonessential government employees and family members to depart Saudi Arabia following an escalation in attacks by the Iranian-backed Houthis.
According to Axios , additional reductions in US diplomatic personnel were ordered at embassies in the United Arab Emirates, Lebanon, Qatar, and Jordan.
CNN also reported on Friday that the United States was accelerating the departure of diplomats and their families from several regional posts, with some personnel having only recently returned following evacuations earlier in the Iran war.
The network further reported that Israel had pressed Washington to launch renewed strikes against Iran sooner, but those efforts had so far been unsuccessful.
The intelligence warning emerged as US President Donald Trump continued to leave open the possibility of additional military action against Iran.
Speaking on Friday, Trump said the United States could launch another operation similar to Operation Epic Fury if Tehran failed to reach an agreement.
“We may do another little Epic Fury. Or they’ll agree,” Trump said.
The latest warning underscores mounting US concerns about the security of American diplomatic personnel as Washington weighs further military action and continues diplomatic efforts to reach an agreement with Iran.

items.title: Oil spill washes up on UAE beaches after tanker strike
items.summary: Satellite images show oil spreading for miles along the coastline, threatening local marine wildlife
items.content:
By Thomas Copeland, Mark Poynting and Tom Spencer BBC Verify
An oil spill from a tanker attacked near the Strait of Hormuz is spreading along the United Arab Emirates (UAE) coastline, forcing the closure of some beaches and coastal areas.
Satellite images from Monday show the beginnings of the oil spill from a ship matching the location and dimensions of Gem No.2, which was damaged between 9 and 10 October during a record surge of vessel strikes by Iran .
The slick of oil had spread more than 35km (22 miles) from the tanker by Wednesday, the satellite imagery showed.
UAE authorities said on Thursday that the incident is affecting beaches near the northern city of Umm Al Quwain and verified video from Friday shows the oil washing ashore, colouring the water black.
The UAE's Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Thursday that it "immediately began containment" in order to "limit environmental impacts".
Prof Steve Widdicombe, director of Sharjah Marine Science Research Centre in the UAE, told BBC Verify it was "inevitable that there will be an impact", but researchers caution it is too soon to assess extent of the damage.
Initially a much smaller oil leak could be seen emerging from the ship on 19 October.
But the slick appears to have rapidly spread over two days, according to radar satellite imagery reviewed by BBC Verify and intelligence firm MAIAR.
Oil spills can cause immediate deaths of marine animals and other organisms, for example by physically trapping turtles, smothering the feathers of seabirds or damaging the gills of fish.
They can also cause longer-lasting damage, Prof Widdicombe said, if species remain exposed to toxic compounds from the oil which could impact their ability to reproduce.
Researchers have cautioned the environmental impact at this stage is very uncertain, as it depends on factors including the volume and type of oil spilled, how quickly it evaporates or breaks down and the effectiveness of the clean-up operation.
But the spill does extend towards Siniyah and Khor Al Beidah islands, a globally recognised Key Biodiversity Area containing habitats like corals, seagrasses and saltmarshes, as well as species including green turtles and the critically endangered Halavi guitarfish.
The proximity of the spill to this area is the "most concerning environmental angle", according to Eoghan Darbyshire, a scientist at the Conflict and Environment Observatory.
BBC Verify analysis of the dimensions and location of the ship indicate they match a crude oil tanker called Gem No.2.
Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard reported the Panama-flagged tanker was "struck by an unknown projectile" on 9 October, just north of the town of Al Jazeera Al Hamra, causing a fire on board that was later extinguished.
Verified footage first posted on social media on 10 October showed the crew running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rose over the ship.
Iranian state media shared footage of a ship matching Gem No.2 which appeared to show the vessel on fire with burning oil spilling into the sea.
The ship had been attempting to exit the Strait of Hormuz via an "unauthorized and dangerous route", according to state media.
All 22 Indian crew members were rescued, the Indian consulate in Dubai said on 11 October.
Gem No.2 is one of a record number of ships that reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz at the start of October .
Security experts told BBC Verify this was part of an Iranian effort to assert greater control over the strait, in response to the US military successfully escorting more vessels through the vital shipping lane.
Tankers and other commercial vessels have come under attack from both Iranian and US forces in and around the Strait of Hormuz amid the conflict between the two countries.
Another major oil slick washed up on the shores of Iran's Qeshm Island in August , which experts said threatened wildlife, protected ecosystems and fishing communities.

Moderna extended losses after plunging nearly 18% on Thursday, while Western Digital fell despite beating earnings expectations and issuing an upbeat outlook.

Retail sentiment on Stocktwits remained weak. Sentiment toward the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), which tracks the S&P 500, trended in 'extremely bearish' territory over the past day. Tehran has vowed to retaliate against any new attacks, potentially targeting economic and civilian infrastructure, the Wall Street Journal reported.
As of 6 a.m. ET, Brent crude futures expiring December were up 1.1% to $114 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures gained 1.6% % to over $101 per barrel.
Meta Platforms (META): Shares dipped 0.6% in early premarket trading on Friday, recovering slightly after falling more than 7% on Thursday, when investors reacted negatively to another increase in the company's annual AI spending forecast and plans to issue new shares to help fund the investment. The sell-off came despite better-than-expected results and a strong forecast, highlighting investor concerns about the scale of AI investments and the prospect of even cash-rich technology companies taking on debt to finance them.
Nvidia (NVDA): The stock edged 0.4% higher in early premarket trading on Friday after ending Thursday's regular session 4.4% down. Adding to concerns over Meta's rising AI spending, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC that "there is a scarcity of capital" for AI infrastructure, adding that "the demand for capital is much greater than the availability."
Advanced Micro Devices (AMD): Shares gained nearly 1% in early premarket trading on Friday, recovering some ground after ending Thursday's session more than 8% lower. Like Meta Platforms and Nvidia, AMD was attempting a rebound after a sharp sell-off in AI-related stocks in the previous session.
CoreWeave (CRWV): The stock was up 2% in premarket trading on Friday after hitting a fresh 17-month low of $53.50 during Thursday's session. Concerns over mounting debt and broader weakness in the AI sector have weighed on the stock. Despite the premarket gains, CRWV was on track for a third straight week of losses as rising borrowing costs and concerns about slowing AI demand continued to weigh on sentiment.
SK Hynix (SKHY): Shares rose almost 5% in premarket trading on Friday. The stock closed 4.4% higher on Thursday, reversing earlier losses of around 3% after the chipmaker halted its review of potential pre-IPO fundraising and listing options for its U.S. subsidiary, Solidigm. According to CNBC, Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for APAC at investment platform eToro, said the recovery suggested concerns over a potential Solidigm IPO had weighed on investor sentiment.
Moderna Inc. (MRNA): Shares fell over 4% in premarket trading on Friday, after Moderna's cancer-vaccine rally hit a setback on Thursday. MRNA is heading for its worst weekly performance in three months, while Mizuho analyst Jared Holz warned that extreme volatility had made the stock a "do-not-trade" for many investors. On Thursday, the shares plunged nearly 18% to close at $202.63, marking their steepest single-day decline in more than two months.
Western Digital Corp. (WDC): The stock was down around 2% in premarket trading despite the company beating fiscal first-quarter earnings expectations. The hard-drive maker delivered stronger profits and an upbeat second-quarter outlook, addressing concerns that the storage boom was losing momentum. However, the upbeat results failed to lift sentiment.

(BE): Shares of the fuel cell maker dropped as much as 2% in premarket trading on Friday after plunging nearly 9% on Thursday and extending losses overnight. The sell-off followed its third-quarter results, which raised concerns over capital expenditure and cash flow.

The Federal Reserve's Latest October Inflation Forecast Has Arrived, and It's Terrible News for Wall Street
Year four of Wall Street's bull market didn't disappoint. The artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out lifted the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI), S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC), and Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) to several record highs throughout 2026.
But expecting the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite to head higher amid persistently elevated inflation is a tall task. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) have quite the challenge on their hands in delivering price stability . Unfortunately, the latest inflation update for October hasn't done policymakers or Wall Street any favors.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and the FOMC may raise rates multiple times in 2027. Image source: Official Federal Reserve Photo.
The Fed's October inflation update is a double whammy for stocks
Though there's no perfect inflation prediction tool, the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland's Inflation Nowcasting tool comes pretty close. The Cleveland Fed's tool provides daily forecasts for current- and forward-month inflation that are updated after the release of relevant economic data.
As of Oct. 20, forecasts for two key inflation measures were headed in the wrong direction.
For starters, we know the Consumer Price Index (CPI) reaccelerated to an annualized 3.7% in September. The Cleveland Fed's inflation tool predicts further acceleration to 3.77% in October. Rapidly rising fuel costs, caused by the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz, likely explain why headline inflation is heading higher.
What's arguably even more worrisome is the projection for Core Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE). Core PCE excludes volatile food and energy costs, providing a comprehensive look at long-term price trends.
After three consecutive months of Core PCE standing pat at 3%, the Inflation Nowcasting tool predicts a steady reacceleration to 3.05% in September (Core PCE for September will be released on the 30th) and 3.13% in October.
The projected uptick in Core PCE suggests that the U.S. economy is dealing with more than just an energy supply shock. Businesses altering their shipping routes and shifting suppliers due to the Iran war are just some of the added costs now affecting the broader economy.
The odds of multiple FOMC rate hikes are climbing, and that's terrible news for stocks
With headline inflation topping the Fed's long-term 2% target for 67 months (and counting), Fed Chair Warsh hasn't minced his words about delivering price stability. On Sept. 16, Warsh and 11 other FOMC members voted unanimously to raise interest rates by a quarter point to 3.75%-4.00%.
With both headline inflation and Core PCE, the latter of which is one of the Fed's preferred price gauges, continuing to move in the wrong direction, the odds are increasing that policymakers will undertake several rate hikes over the next year.
According to the CME Group 's (NASDAQ:CME) proprietary FedWatch Tool, which uses 30-day Fed Funds futures to track the probability of changes to the federal funds target rate, there's a 72% probability that interest rates will rise by at least 75 basis points to 4.50%-4.75% by Sept. 15, 2027.
An aggressive Fed rate-hiking cycle would be awful news for a historically expensive, AI-driven bull market. If borrowing becomes costlier and the AI infrastructure build-out slows, even slightly, this could be enough of a catalyst to send a pricey stock market lower rather quickly.

items.title: Brent crude oil tops $116, a six-month high, as tensions swell in the Middle East
items.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump accused Iran on Thursday of trying to manipulate the oil market.
items.content:
Iran's army chief said Tehran is fully prepared for "asymmetric warfare" after strengthening its capabilities, according to the state media agency Tasnim.
Traders expect the U.S. to resume strikes on Iran in the coming weeks.
Iran-allied Houthi militants keep targeting Saudi Arabia.
Sen: Middle East escalation is a matter of ‘when’, not ‘if'
Brent crude oil rose to a six-month high on Friday, as investors increasingly expect the U.S. to resume strikes on Iran in the coming weeks.
Brent futures gained 3.1% to close at $116.72 a barrel, the highest settlement for the international benchmark since April 29. U.S. West Texas Intermediate added 3.8% to settle at $103.27 a barrel.
Iran's army chief, meanwhile, said the country's military is fully prepared for "asymmetric warfare" after strengthening its capabilities, according to the state media agency Tasnim .
Brent added 6.2% for the week, the third consecutive week of gains. WTI advanced 2% for the week.
President Donald Trump said Wednesday that the U.S. was not negotiating with Iran and something would happen "fairly soon." His cryptic remarks came as U.S. officials told The New York Times that the U.S. and Israel have plans for fresh strikes on Iran after the midterm elections.
Iran-allied Houthi militants have continued to strike Saudi Arabia.The U.S. State Department has ordered all non-essential personnel to leave Saudi Arabia due to the strikes.
A drone attack targeting the Shaybah oil field Wednesday in the Eastern Region left two people dead and two injured, according to Saudi state media. At least two people were killed and eight injured in an attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on Wednesday.
Oil giant Saudi Aramco have told staff to evacuate its Dhahran headquarters and work remotely following a series of attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels, Reuters reported .

items.title: Hospital in Yemen’s Taiz warns of collapse in days because of Houthi siege
items.summary: Dialysis patients face shorter treatment sessions as severe shortages of fuel, medicines, and oxygen threaten hospitals.
items.content:
Share Hospital in Yemen’s Taiz warns of collapse in days because of Houthi siege on social media
Signs of battles between Yemeni government forces and Iran-backed Houthis west of Taiz on Wednesday [AFP]
Taiz, Yemen – It was approaching 10:30am in the dialysis centre of the Republican Hospital in Taiz when a machine began filtering excess fluids, toxins and salts from the blood of Omar Mukhtar Hammoud.
The 16-year-old suffers from kidney failure and is one of 270 patients who regularly receive dialysis at the centre in the government-held city in southwest Yemen. But with essential medical supplies and fuel running critically low under the renewed Houthi siege , doctors fear they may soon be unable to provide the treatment that keeps their patients alive.

Dr Essam Mahyoub Dahan, the centre’s director, warned that a complete shutdown could happen within days.
“Because of the siege and the shortage of diesel and medical solutions, we have recently been forced to reduce dialysis sessions from four hours to just two and a half,” Dahan told Al Jazeera. “We know this is not adequate, but we have no choice if we are to keep the centre operating for as long as possible before it shuts down completely.”
Dahan said the centre’s remaining stocks of specialised dialysis solutions were also close to running out.
The supplies, which are expensive, are normally provided by the Yemeni Ministry of Health every three months. But the latest delivery which was due earlier this month  failed to arrive because of the Houthi siege on Taiz city. It began in the first week of October after Houthi advances in the Taiz countryside.
The city was previously under complete Houthi siege between 2015 and 2016, in the early years of Yemen’s ongoing war.
Across Taiz governorate, where battles are raging between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Iranian-allied Houthi fighters, the number of patients at risk is far greater.
In an October 12 statement, the governorate’s health office warned that the continued siege and obstruction of essential supplies could endanger the lives of 1,110 patients with kidney failure. They depend on dialysis services in the governorate’s hospitals, which collectively provide about 210 dialysis sessions a day.
International humanitarian and health organisations have issued similar warnings about the impact of the siege on the already fragile healthcare system in Taiz.
On Thursday, Amnesty International called on the Houthis to immediately reopen vital roads into and around the city, warning that the closure of the main road between Taiz and the southern port city of Aden threatened hundreds of thousands of civilians with losing access to food, water and healthcare.
Taiz’s hospitals depend heavily on diesel-powered generators because much of the city’s electricity infrastructure was destroyed during the war that began 11 years ago and has not been restored.
The renewed Houthi siege has severely disrupted the entry of fuel, including the diesel needed to run hospital generators and lifesaving medical equipment.
Dr Shaheed al-Ameri, deputy director-general for technical affairs at the Republican Hospital, said the shortages have had a devastating impact on medical services.
“A very large part of this suffering is because of the shortage of diesel,” he told Al Jazeera. “We have no reserve diesel supplies. Our stocks ran out early in the siege and we are now buying it on the black market almost every day, at prices that have reached five times what they were before the siege.”
Al-Ameri warned that the longer the siege continues, the more prices will rise and the further medical services will deteriorate.
The hospital has already suspended operations in some departments, including essential units, he said.
“If this situation continues much longer, we fear we will reach a complete and comprehensive collapse of healthcare services,” he said.
The shortages are not confined to the Republican Hospital. On October 22, the World Health Organization (WHO) warned that critical shortages of fuel, oxygen, medicines and medical supplies were threatening lifesaving healthcare throughout  Taiz governorate, with some hospital services already disrupted.
According to the WHO, 42 health facilities in Taiz city had reported severe shortages of essential supplies. Hospitals and ambulances require at least 156,000 litres of fuel a month to continue functioning.
The organisation also warned that diesel shortages threaten to disrupt oxygen production, water pumping, vaccine refrigeration and sanitation services, increasing the risks of disease outbreaks, particularly among displaced families and other vulnerable groups.
The United Nations has separately warned that the restrictions on supplies are bringing Taiz’s health system close to collapse and urged the Houthis to allow humanitarian assistance and essential goods to enter without obstruction.
In its October 12 statement, Taiz’s health office warned that continued restrictions on fuel deliveries could lead to the shutdown of medical oxygen production plants, further endangering patients.
Taysir al-Samei, the health office’s media officer, said that would dramatically worsen the crisis.
“Many medical departments depend on oxygen, particularly operating theatres, inpatient wards, intensive care units and incubators for premature babies,” al-Samei said.
“Most hospitals have already suspended services in some units because of the shortage of diesel and the lack of necessary medical solutions, as well as shortages of medical staff who are struggling to get to work because of the lack of transport,” he added.
He warned that if conditions continued to deteriorate at the same pace, some hospitals could stop providing services in the coming days.
At the Republican Hospital, al-Ameri said that shortages were also affecting diagnostics and treatment. The availability of laboratory reagents had fallen to just 10 to 15 percent of previous levels, he said, while approximately half of the medicines normally available were now out of stock.
Prices for the remaining medicines had doubled, he said, placing them further out of reach for patients already struggling with Yemen’s worsening economic crisis.
The continued fighting and shelling around Taiz have increased the number of wounded people requiring emergency care – placing additional pressure on facilities already struggling with shortages of surgical supplies , anaesthetics and intravenous fluids.
Abdul Badi Abdulwuhab, 53, is another dialysis patient in the Republican Hospital, struggling to cope with the shorter dialysis sessions.
“Because of these measures, I suffer from weakness and I cannot bear the pain,” Abdul Badi told Al Jazeera. “Two and a half hours is not enough to remove all the fluids and toxins from my body.”
Dr Dahan said that the patient’s condition had deteriorated since his sessions were shortened.
“These measures are not effective for many patients,” Dahan said. “The only solution is to end the siege and return things to the way they were.”
